idiom_name: sqlite3 connection in WAL mode + queue.Queue drained by one writer thread
implementation_notes: The standard library is the store: sqlite3.connect with explicit transaction control (isolation_level=None plus BEGIN IMMEDIATE/COMMIT, or the autocommit attribute on newer interpreters) decides when a record is durable, PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL lets reporting readers run while the writer appends, and executemany batches the copy so the fsync cost is amortised. The tap is a queue.Queue drained by one writer thread, or asyncio.to_thread from a coroutine, so the request path only enqueues - which is what replaces the classic Store object and interceptor. Retention is a DELETE plus periodic VACUUM on a timer, and reporting queries the same file, ideally through a read-only connection. A SQLAlchemy model over Postgres is the same shape at larger scale; a hand-written Store interface is only justified when several backends must be pluggable.
pitfalls: sqlite3 connections are per-thread by default (check_same_thread): the writer-thread design avoids the problem entirely, whereas disabling the check without your own lock corrupts the connection.

With isolation_level left at its default the module's implicit transactions can stay open across statements, so the retention job and the writer collide with 'database is locked'; WAL plus short explicit transactions is the fix.
A queue is process-local: a crash of the writer thread loses whatever is still queued, so count and alert on it - otherwise the audit trail's gap is invisible.
json.dumps of arbitrary payloads can raise or be slow on the request path; serialise in the writer, or store the bytes you already received.
